cues.text: An Orphan Who Chose the Church Over Comfort
Richard was born around 1197 at Wyche, near Droitwich in Worcestershire, England, the second son of Richard and Alice de Wyche.
His father died while he was still a boy, and the family estate, mismanaged in his father's absence, fell into serious disrepair.

Rather than accept his brother's offer to make over the whole inheritance to him, or a marriage that would have secured his fortune, Richard chose instead to restore the estate to profitability with his own hands.
He then walked away from it entirely, setting off for Oxford to study.
At Oxford, and later at Paris and Bologna, he lived for a time in such poverty that he and two companions shared a single tunic and gown between them, attending lectures by turns.
He earned a doctorate in law at Bologna before returning to England, where his talents as a scholar and administrator quickly drew notice.
Chancellor to Two Archbishops

Richard's education and evident integrity brought him first to the chancellorship of Oxford University in 1235, and soon after to the household of Edmund of Abingdon, Archbishop of Canterbury, as his chancellor.

When Edmund went into exile in France rather than yield to King Henry III on the rights of the Church, Richard followed him, remaining at his side at the Cistercian abbey of Pontigny until Edmund's death.
Richard then studied for the priesthood among the Dominicans at Orleans and was ordained in 1243.
Returning to England, he served for a time as a parish priest before the new Archbishop of Canterbury, Boniface of Savoy, called him back into service as his own chancellor.
A Bishopric Fought Over by a King
When the see of Chichester fell vacant, King Henry III moved to install his own candidate, Ralph Neville, the royal chancellor.
Archbishop Boniface declared the appointment invalid and named Richard instead, an act that provoked the king's fury.

Pope Innocent IV upheld Richard's election in 1245, but Henry, undeterred, barred him from his own episcopal palace and revenues for years afterward, forcing Richard to live for a time on the charity of a sympathetic priest.
Only the threat of excommunication finally moved the king to relent.
A Reforming Bishop
Once in possession of his see, Richard governed with a severity toward vice matched only by his tenderness toward the poor.

He demanded strict discipline of his clergy, denounced corruption wherever he found it, in the royal court as readily as in the Church, and gave generously from what little his years of dispossession had left him.

Tradition remembers him, too, for a small and telling wonder: that he once dropped the chalice during Mass and nothing spilled from it, an image later artists placed at his feet in nearly every portrait of him.
Death on the Road to Dover

In 1252, Pope Innocent IV commissioned Richard to preach in favor of a new crusade, and he threw himself into the task with characteristic energy, traveling through the Dioceses of Chichester and Canterbury to rouse support for the cause.
While journeying to Dover to consecrate a new church dedicated to St. Edmund, he fell ill.
He reached the town, completed the consecration on 2 April, and died the following morning, 3 April 1253, in a hospital for poor priests called the Maison Dieu.
His body was carried back to Chichester and buried in the cathedral he had served.
Legacy
Miracles reported at Richard's tomb led Pope Urban IV to canonize him in 1262.
In 1276, his relics were translated to a shrine that became one of medieval England's great pilgrimage centers.
Thomas Cromwell ordered it plundered and destroyed in 1538.
What survived every upheaval was a short prayer tradition has long attributed to him.
It later found new voice in the musical Godspell: "Thanks be to Thee, my Lord Jesus Christ, for all the benefits Thou hast given me, for all the pains and insults which Thou hast borne for me.
O most merciful Redeemer, Friend, and Brother, may I know Thee more clearly, love Thee more dearly, and follow Thee more nearly, day by day."

We recognize in Richard a bishop who never let dispossession curdle into bitterness, choosing instead, at every turn, the poorer and more difficult road, a pattern any believer facing injustice might still take as its own kind of prayer.
